title: One number for many
objectives: Find the mean, median, mode and range of a data set, and read them from a table or a chart.

screens.prose: A trader's profits over seven days, in pounds: 120, $-80$, 40, 40, 300, $-60$ and 60. Each block sits at its profit on the line; the two 40s stack. Drag the pivot under the line until the chart would balance.

derive.caption: Pivot at £{{round(pivot)}}: distance of days below it £{{round(max(0, pivot + 80) + max(0, pivot + 60) + 2 * max(0, pivot - 40) + max(0, pivot - 60) + max(0, pivot - 120) + max(0, pivot - 300))}}, above it £{{round(max(0, -80 - pivot) + max(0, -60 - pivot) + 2 * max(0, 40 - pivot) + max(0, 60 - pivot) + max(0, 120 - pivot) + max(0, 300 - pivot))}}

screens.question: Drag the pivot to the balance point.

hints.text: Balance means the distances below the pivot add up to the distances above it.
Watch the caption: move the pivot until the two distances match.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the pivot until the two distances in the caption are equal.

byKey.middle: At £40 the distance above is bigger than below. The £300 day pulls the balance higher.
byKey.centre-axis: That is the middle of the axis, not the balance point. Read the caption.
byKey.pivot: Keep moving: the two distances in the caption must match.

explain.text: At £60 the days below sit $140 + 120 + 20 + 20 = 300$ pounds away and the days above $60 + 240 = 300$ away. The total, £420, shared over 7 days is also £60. The balance point is the share each day would get.

screens.prose: Now put the same seven days in order of profit.

state.caption: The seven days in the order they happened

screens.question: Drag the profits into order, smallest first.

hints.text: Losses come first, and the bigger loss is smaller.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the biggest loss, end with the biggest profit.

byKey.t6: −£60 comes after −£80: a loss of £80 is the smaller number.
byKey.t2: −£80 is the smallest: it is the biggest loss.

explain.text: On the number line, $-80 < -60 < 40 = 40 < 60 < 120 < 300$. A bigger loss is a smaller number.

screens.prose: The balance point, £60, is the **mean**: the total shared equally, $420 \div 7$. Here are the days in order.

state.caption: The seven days, smallest to largest

screens.question: Tap the middle day.

hints.text: Seven days: how many sit on each side of the middle one?
Three days below and three above.

feedback.correct: The fourth day, £40, is in the middle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count three days in from either end.

byKey.d5: £60 is the mean. The middle day is the fourth of seven.
byKey.d3: That bar is third of seven. The middle is fourth, which also reads £40.
byKey.d1: That is the smallest day. Count three in from each end.

explain.text: Three days sit below the fourth and three above, so the middle value is £40. It is lower than the mean, £60, because the £300 day pulls the mean up but not the middle.

screens.prose: The middle value of a sorted list is the **median**: £40. The most common value is the **mode**: £40 again. The **range** is the largest minus the smallest: it measures spread, not a typical day.
screens.question: What is the range of the seven profits?

hints.text: Take the smallest away from the largest.
Taking away a negative adds: $300 + 80$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the smallest value, $-80$, from the largest.

byKey.sign: You worked out $300 - 80$. The smallest is $-80$, and taking away $-80$ adds 80.
byKey.count: 7 is the number of days. The range is a difference of profits.

explain.text: Range = largest − smallest = $300 - (-80) = 380$ pounds. Taking away a negative adds (level 2). The days spread over £380.

screens.prose: Suppose the £300 day had been £3,100 instead. The other six days stay the same.
screens.question: Find the new mean and the new median.

hints.text: The total rises by $3{,}100 - 300 = 2{,}800$.
New total $420 + 2{,}800 = 3{,}220$, shared over 7 days.
The middle day of the sorted list has not moved.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recompute the total for the mean; find the middle for the median.

byKey.unchanged: The mean uses every value, so changing one day changes it: $3{,}220 \div 7 = 460$.
byKey.total: That is the new total. Share it over 7 days.
byKey.moved: The median is the middle day, not the mean. It is still the fourth day, £40.
byKey.big: £3,100 is the largest day, not the middle one.

explain.text: The total becomes £3,220, so the mean jumps to $3{,}220 \div 7 = 460$. The middle day is still the fourth, £40. One extreme day moves the mean a lot and the median not at all.

screens.prose: With an even number of values there is no single middle one. Four days made 3, 5, 8 and 10 trades.
screens.question: What is the median number of trades?

hints.text: The two middle values are 5 and 8.
Take the mean of the middle two.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the two middle values and go halfway between them.

byKey.lower: 5 is the lower of the two middle values. Go halfway to 8.
byKey.upper: 8 is the upper of the two middle values. Go halfway to 5.
byKey.no-half: You added the middle two. Halve the sum.

explain.text: The middle two values are 5 and 8, so the median is $(5 + 8) \div 2 = 6.5$. No day made 6.5 trades: a median or mean need not be a possible value.

screens.prose: A desk counted trades per day over 20 days: 0 trades on 2 days, 1 on 5, 2 on 8, 3 on 4 and 4 on 1.
screens.question: Fill in the table.

hints.text: Total trades: each trade count times its days, added up.
$0 \times 2 + 1 \times 5 + 2 \times 8 + 3 \times 4 + 4 \times 1$.
The 10th and 11th days, in order, both made 2 trades.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each trade count by its number of days.

byKey.added-values: You added 0 to 4. Each count happens on several days: weight it.
byKey.days: 20 is the number of days. Count the trades.
byKey.per-row: You divided by the 5 rows. Divide by the 20 days.
byKey.freq-mean: You averaged the bar heights. Divide the trades by the days.
byKey.tallest: 8 is the height of the tallest bar, a number of days. The median is a number of trades.
byKey.count: 8 is how many days made 2 trades. The mode is the trade count itself, 2.

explain.text: Total $0 + 5 + 16 + 12 + 4 = 37$ trades over 20 days, so the mean is $37 \div 20 = 1.85$. The 10th and 11th days in order both made 2, so the median is 2. The tallest bar makes the mode 2.

screens.prose: Five days have a mean profit of £60. Four of them were £120, $-$£80, £40 and £40.
screens.question: What did Friday make?

hints.text: A mean of £60 over 5 days means a total of $5 \times 60$.
The four days add to $120 - 80 + 40 + 40 = 120$.
Friday is the total less 120.

feedback.correct: The total is £300, the four days make £120, so Friday made £180.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the total from the mean first.

byKey.mean: £60 is the average. Friday must make up what the other four days lack.
byKey.total: £300 is the five-day total. Take away the four known days.
byKey.four-days: You used $4 \times 60 = 240$. The mean is over 5 days: $5 \times 60 = 300$.

explain.text: Mean × days gives the total: $60 \times 5 = 300$ pounds. The four known days add to £120, so Friday made $300 - 120 = 180$ pounds.

screens.prose: Two teams' average pay: 10 traders average £50,000, and 30 traders average £70,000. A manager quotes £60,000 for all 40.
screens.question: What is the true average pay of all 40 traders?

hints.text: Find the total pay of each team first.
Share the combined total over 40 traders.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two totals, then divide by 40.

byKey.simple: Like the manager, you averaged the two averages. The bigger team counts three times as much.
byKey.added: You added the averages. Total the pay, then share it over 40.

explain.text: The totals are £500,000 and £2,100,000, so all 40 earn £2,600,000. That gives $2{,}600{,}000 \div 40 = 65{,}000$. Averaging the two averages gives the small team as much weight as the big one.

screens.prose: A chart compares a desk's profit last year, £50,000, with this year, £55,000. Look where its axis starts.
screens.question: How many times as large is this year's profit as last year's?

hints.text: Read the values, not the bar heights.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the two values, not the two bar heights.

byKey.bars: You compared the bar heights. The axis starts at £45,000, so the bars show only the part above it.

explain.text: The bars show 5,000 and 10,000 above the £45,000 start, so one looks twice the other. The true ratio is $55{,}000 \div 50{,}000 = 1.1$. A cut-off axis makes small changes look big.

screens.prose: Why is the mean the balance point? Use the seven days: total £420, mean £60.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order. Leave out the line that does not follow.

lines.text: Sharing the total, £420, equally over 7 days gives each day £60: the mean.
Write each day as £60 plus its distance above the mean, or minus its distance below.
Adding the seven days: 420 is $7 \times 60$, plus the distances above, minus the distances below.
Since $7 \times 60 = 420$, the distances above minus the distances below come to 0.
So they balance. Check: below, $140 + 120 + 20 + 20 = 300$; above, $60 + 240 = 300$.
So half the days lie above the mean.
lines.why: That describes the median. Here only 2 of the 7 days lie above the mean.

hints.text: Start from what the mean is.
Each day is the mean plus or minus a distance.
Share, write, add, cancel, check.

feedback.correct: The distances on each side of the mean add to the same amount, £300.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line should follow from the one before.

byKey.half: Half the days above is the median's property. Only 2 days lie above £60.

explain.text: Each day is the mean plus or minus a distance. Adding all seven gives the total plus the distances above minus those below, so those two must cancel. On the seven days both sides come to £300.

screens.prose: A fund's weekly note says: "Average daily profit £460." The week was the seven days with the £3,100 day: $-80$, $-60$, 40, 40, 60, 120 and 3,100.
screens.question: Which figure answers "what does a typical day look like?"

options.why: £460 is the mean the note quotes. Six of the seven days made far less: one day drags it up.
The range measures spread, not a typical day.
£60 was the mean before the big day. This week's mean is £460.

hints.text: Which average is the note quoting?
$3{,}220 \div 7 = 460$: the note quotes the mean.
Which average ignores how big the biggest day is?

feedback.correct: The median, £40: four of the seven days made £40 or less.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the average one big day cannot drag.

byKey.mean: The mean is honest arithmetic but not a typical day: six days made £120 or less.

explain.text: The note's £460 is the mean, pulled up by one £3,100 day. The median, £40, says what a typical day looked like. Later courses measure the spread around the centre as well as the centre itself.

ideas: The mean shares the total equally and is the balance point; one extreme value can drag it far.
The median is the middle of the sorted values (the mean of the middle two for an even count); the mode is the most common.
The range, largest minus smallest, measures spread; a frequency table weights each value by its count.

formula.name: Mean
formula.note: From a frequency table: total = each value times its count, added up.

summary.trap: Averaging two averages ignores group sizes: 10 at £50,000 and 30 at £70,000 average £65,000, not £60,000.

quiz.prose: Trades per day over a week: 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 7, 9.
quiz.question: What is the mode?

options.why: 3 and 7 each appear twice, more than any other value.
5 is the median, the middle value.

feedback.correct: 3 and 7 both appear twice: two modes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how often each value appears.

explain.text: 3 and 7 each appear twice and every other value once, so the data has two modes. A list where every value appears once has no mode.

quiz.prose: A histogram of 14 trade sizes, in shares.
quiz.question: What does the tallest bar tell you?

options.why: A histogram bar covers a range of sizes, not one size.
The height counts trades; the biggest trade, 410, is in the last bar.
The height counts trades, not shares.

feedback.correct: 6 trades fell in the 200 to 300 range.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. In a histogram a bar's width is a range and its height a count.

explain.text: Each bar covers a range of sizes, and its height counts the trades in that range. The tallest bar says 6 trades were between 200 and 300 shares.

quiz.question: What is the mean daily profit?

feedback.correct: The total is £100, so the mean is £20.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the five values, counting losses as negative, then divide by 5.

byKey.ignored-signs: You added the losses as gains. $-20$ and $-40$ lower the total.
byKey.total: £100 is the total. Share it over 5 days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the smallest, $-30$, from the largest, 40.

byKey.sign: You worked out $40 - 30$. The smallest is $-30$; taking it away adds 30.
byKey.first-last: You used the first and last values listed. Use the largest and smallest.

explain.text: The largest is 40 and the smallest $-30$, so the range is $40 - (-30) = 70$ pounds.
